atoms.title: Andersonia West renamed Tc'ih-Léh-Dûñ (Fish Run Place)

atoms.text: Before the arrival of white settlers in the 19th century, the Sinkyone people had travelled, hunted and fished in California for thousands of years. Upon their arrival in the Sinkyone’s regions, white settlers began logging in the forest to satisfy the demand for lumber and resources at the time. Due to such exploitation, a mere five percent of the original old-growth redwood forest remain on the West Coast of the USA to this day.
atoms.sound: Before the arrival of white settlers in the 19th century, the Sinkyown people had travelled, hunted and fished in California for thousands of years. Upon their arrival in the Sinkyown’s regions, white settlers began logging in the forest to satisfy the demand for lumber and resources at the time. Due to such exploitation, a mere five percent of the original old-growth redwood forest remain on the West Coast of the USA to this day.

atoms.text: Now, the Sinkyone tribe have rightfully been given back 523 acres of their ancestral lands by a non-profit league who vouch for the protection and restoration of the redwood forests. Furthermore, the area has been renamed back to its original name: Tc'ih-Léh-Dûñ. Representatives from the InterTribal Sinkyone Wilderness Council and Save the Redwoods League plan on preserving the forest, so its beauty may be enjoyed by many generations to come.
atoms.sound: Now, the Sinkyown tribe have rightfully been given back 523 acres of their ancestral lands by a non-profit league who vouch for the protection and restoration of the redwood forests. Furthermore, the area has been renamed back to its original name: ti-e-laydon. Representatives from the InterTribal Sinkyown Wilderness Council and Save the Redwoods League plan on preserving the forest, so its beauty may be enjoyed by many generations to come.
